# Diagnosing Right-Side Drift in Grand Voyager Minivans

When a vehicle pulls to the right immediately after releasing the accelerator, you are observing a specific aerodynamic and mechanical imbalance often referred to as off-axle drag. In your temporary Grand Voyager, this manifests because the left side of the chassis is encountering slightly more resistance than the right, causing the vehicle to pivot toward the lower-resistance path. While many drivers dismiss this as normal wear, in an older minivan with high ground clearance and significant frontal area, it often signals a specific maintenance gap rather than catastrophic failure.

The most common culprit in vehicles of this age and profile is uneven tire pressure or tread depth. When you let go of the gas, the engine torque drops to zero, leaving inertia as the only driving force. At that moment, any difference in rolling resistance becomes amplified. If the left tires have lower pressure than the right, they deform more against the road surface, creating higher friction. This effectively acts like a brake on the left side, yanking the front of the car to the right. The steering correction you are making is simply compensating for this lateral force vector.

To verify this, you need to check tire pressure with a calibrated gauge, not just rely on the dashboard sensor which can lag or be inaccurate. Rotate the tires if possible to see if the pull persists; if the issue moves with the wheels, it confirms a tire-related problem. Tread depth is equally critical. On an old Grand Voyager, uneven wear patterns—such as cupping or scalloping—can create significant drag differences even at matched pressures. A tread depth check using a standard gauge should reveal discrepancies greater than 1/32 of an inch between opposite wheels.

Another frequent cause in older minivans is steering linkage play, specifically within the tie rod ends and ball joints. As these components age, internal clearance increases. When driving straight under load (acceleration), this slack takes up space without affecting geometry. However, when torque is released, the suspension settles into a neutral position where any lateral play in the left side's linkage can shift the wheel alignment momentarily toward the right. This feels like a pull but is actually a geometric drift caused by worn bushings or joints.

You should also inspect the brake drag condition. If the left front caliper piston is sticking slightly, it applies constant friction to the rotor even when the pedal is released. This creates a "brake-on" scenario on one side only, pulling the vehicle hard toward the right upon deceleration. A simple test involves lifting the car and spinning each wheel by hand; excessive resistance on one side compared to the other indicates caliper or wheel cylinder issues that require bench rebuilding or replacement.

While this symptom is rarely a sign of immediate safety failure, it increases stopping distances and causes uneven tire wear. Addressing it early prevents expensive repairs down the road.
